configFields.label: Broker URL
configFields.description: MQTT broker URL, e.g. mqtt://localhost:1883, mqtts://host:8883, or ws://host:9001.

configFields.label: Topics
configFields.description: Topic filter(s) to subscribe to. Comma-separate several; MQTT wildcards + (single level) and # (multi level) are allowed, e.g. home/+/temperature, sensors/#.

configFields.label: QoS
configFields.description: Subscription quality of service: 0 (at most once), 1 (at least once), or 2 (exactly once). Defaults to 1.

tours.title: Start a process from a broker message
tours.blurb: Wire an MQTT topic to a process start — the “when this happens…” half of an automation.

steps.title: An MQTT message can start a process
steps.body: Installing this pack adds a trigger source kind, `mqtt`, that any App can declare in its `nano.app.json`. You name a broker and a topic filter; the runtime owns the durable inbox, dispatch, retry and lifecycle, and auto-launches this pack's driver (ADR 0025). Each message can start a process or correlate into a running one.

steps.title: Run the app so the driver starts
steps.body: The trigger driver is a supervised out-of-process child of your running app — nothing subscribes until the app is running.

repair.title: Install a JavaScript runtime first
repair.body: Running an app needs Node ≥ 22.6 (the npm launcher ships one) or Deno. Until then you can still author the trigger — only starting it is unavailable.

steps.title: Publish a test message
steps.body: Any MQTT client will do — this step is outside the console because the broker is. Adjust the topic to match the filter you declared.

steps.title: See what the message started
steps.body: The message that arrived is now a process instance, and its payload is the instance's variables — an event your process can reason about.
